items: Distinguish a traditional monolith from a modular monolith and know when each is appropriate.
Understand the trade-offs between deployment simplicity and architectural boundaries.
Apply module boundaries, explicit dependencies, and build-time enforcement to a monolith.
Recognize the warning signs that indicate a monolith should be decomposed.
Monolith — a single deployable unit containing all application logic, often sharing one database and one process.
Modular Monolith — a single deployable that is internally organized into well-isolated modules with explicit, enforced contracts.
Module Boundary — a logical seam that restricts which code may depend on which, enforced at compile/link time.
Shared Kernel — a small, explicitly agreed-upon subset of code shared between modules (use sparingly).
Deployment Coupling — the property that changing one part forces redeploying the whole system.
Architecture Fitness Function — an automated check that guards a desired architectural property (e.g., "module A must not import module B").

blocks.text: A "monolith" is frequently used as a pejorative, but it simply means the system ships as one artifact (a JAR, WAR, binary, or single process tree) and runs in one deployment unit. This is not inherently bad. A well-built monolith is easy to develop, test, debug, and deploy: a single codebase, one transaction boundary, and one database make reasoning about consistency trivial. Teams can move fast when they do not have to worry about network calls, distributed transactions, or service versioning.
The Problem: The Big Ball of Mud

The failure mode of monoliths is not "being one unit" but unstructured coupling. Over time, layers blur: a controller calls a repository in another feature, a domain object reaches into another domain's tables, and a "small change" ripples across the entire codebase. This is the "big ball of mud" — an architecture defined only by expedience. The cost is not the deployment model; it is the absence of boundaries.

A modular monolith keeps the single-deployable advantage but introduces strict internal modules. Each module owns its domain logic and data access; dependencies between modules are explicit and directed (a DAG, never a cycle). Communication across module boundaries happens through published interfaces, not through shared mutable state. The database may still be shared physically, but each module logically owns its tables/schema.
Boundaries that exist only on a whiteboard rot quickly. Use build tooling to enforce them:

items: Java: ArchUnit, or module-info.java (JPMS).
.NET: internal access modifiers + Roslyn analyzers.
JavaScript/TS: ESLint no-restricted-imports or import boundaries via depcheck.
A CI "fitness function" fails the build when a forbidden dependency is introduced.

blocks.text: When to Stay Modular, When to Split

A modular monolith is the right default for most teams and most of a product's life. It gives you many microservice benefits (team autonomy, clear ownership) without distributed-system costs. Move to separate services only when you have a concrete driver: independent scalability of one component, independent deploy frequency, or a hard technology mismatch. A modular monolith is also the safest intermediate step before extracting microservices — the boundaries you enforce now become your future service seams.
